claims.text: Steady-state creep rate in nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings is governed by the degree of interface coherence at FCC/BCC boundaries.
Interfacial short-range order governs the steady-state creep rate.
Greater interface coherence and short-range order raise the barrier to interface-mediated dislocation climb and thereby slow creep.
The starting multilayer has 20 nm FCC and BCC layers.
The as-deposited multilayer has semi-coherent interfaces.
In the starting material, short-range order occurs only within the individual layers.
The proposed intervention is post-deposition annealing at 700 °C for 1 h under an inert atmosphere.
Annealing at 700 °C for 1 h will enhance FCC/BCC interface coherence by reducing the density of misfit dislocations.
Annealing at 700 °C for 1 h will promote short-range chemical order at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Enhanced interface coherence and interfacial short-range order increase lattice friction.
Enhanced interface coherence and interfacial short-range order impede dislocation climb across FCC/BCC interfaces.
Impeded cross-interface dislocation climb forces dislocations to pile up.
Dislocation pileups slow incremental plastic strain under sustained load.
At 600 °C and 500 MPa, the annealed multilayer will have an approximately 50% lower steady-state creep rate than the as-deposited baseline over 100 h.
The semi-coherent baseline has a steady-state creep rate of approximately 1×10^-5 h^-1 at 600 °C and 500 MPa.
The proposed mechanism is valid for layer thicknesses of 5–50 nm, temperatures of 400–700 °C, and stresses of 200–800 MPa.
Outside the stated thickness, temperature, and stress ranges, other creep mechanisms such as lattice-diffusion creep may dominate.
A steady-state creep-rate difference of less than 10% between the annealed and as-deposited samples would falsify the hypothesis.
